steps.body: A **regular shape** (every side and angle equal) has exactly as many symmetry lines as it has sides. An equilateral triangle: 3 sides, 3 symmetry lines. A square: 4 sides, 4 symmetry lines. A regular pentagon: 5 sides, 5 symmetry lines.
Compare side counts and symmetry-line counts for regular shapes.

widget.prompt: Inspect the three regular shapes. Which rule matches every row?

choices.label: Lines equal sides
choices.feedback: Each displayed regular shape has one symmetry line for each side.

choices.label: Lines are always fewer
choices.feedback: The rows show equal counts, not fewer symmetry lines.
choices.evidenceText: The square has 4 sides and 4 lines.

choices.label: Lines are always more
choices.feedback: The rows show equal counts, not extra symmetry lines.
choices.evidenceText: The triangle has 3 sides and 3 lines.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Compare each pair of counts: 3 and 3, 4 and 4, 5 and 5.
widget.successFeedback: For these regular polygons, the symmetry-line count matches the side count.

predict.prompt: For a REGULAR shape, how does its number of symmetry lines compare to its number of sides?
predict.reveal: Perfect regularity buys one mirror line per side — a regular pentagon carries five, a regular hexagon six. The count of sides IS the count of mirrors.

explanationVariants: A regular hexagon has 6 sides, so it has 6 lines of symmetry.
The side count and symmetry count always match for regular shapes.

widget.prompt: A regular hexagon has 6 equal sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 would be half the sides. For a REGULAR shape, the symmetry count matches the full side count: 6.
12 doubles the side count. For a regular shape, symmetry lines equal the side count exactly: 6.

widget.fallbackFeedback: For a regular shape, count the sides — that's also the symmetry-line count.

steps.body: Shapes that AREN'T regular can have fewer symmetry lines. A rectangle (unequal sides) has only **2** — the horizontal and vertical center lines. Its diagonals do NOT produce a match, since folding along one would need the two different side lengths to line up, which they can't.

explanationVariants: A rectangle (not a square) has exactly 2 lines of symmetry — its diagonals don't work.
Only the horizontal and vertical center lines produce a match.

widget.prompt: A rectangle is 8 units long and 3 units wide (not a square). How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 would be right for a SQUARE, where all sides are equal. This rectangle's unequal sides mean its diagonals don't work — only 2 lines.
0 undercounts — the horizontal and vertical center lines both still produce a match. That's 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Only the horizontal and vertical center lines work for a non-square rectangle.

widget.prompt: Sort each shape by how many lines of symmetry it has.

items.label: A scalene triangle (no equal sides)
items.feedback: Zero matching sides means zero fold lines can produce a match.

items.label: A rectangle (unequal sides)
items.feedback: Only the horizontal and vertical center lines work — 2 lines.

widget.missFeedback: Check whether the shape is regular (all sides equal, matching the side count) or has some other structure.
widget.successFeedback: Scalene triangles have none; rectangles have 2; equilateral triangles and squares have 3 or more.

explanationVariants: An isosceles triangle (exactly two equal sides) has exactly 1 line of symmetry, through the top point and the middle of the unequal side.
Only one fold works here, unlike the 3 lines of a fully equal-sided triangle.

widget.prompt: A triangle has exactly two equal sides (and one different side). How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 would be right for an EQUILATERAL triangle, where all three sides are equal. With only two sides equal, there's just 1 line of symmetry.
0 undercounts — the two equal sides still allow one fold, through the top point and the base's middle: 1 line.

widget.fallbackFeedback: With exactly two equal sides, only one fold line (through the top point) produces a match.

hints: A regular octagon has 8 equal sides.
The symmetry-line pattern for a regular shape matches its side count.
explanationVariants: A regular octagon's 8 equal sides give it exactly 8 lines of symmetry.
The regular-shape pattern (sides = symmetry lines) applies here too.

widget.prompt: A stained-glass window is shaped like a regular octagon (8 equal sides). How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 would be half the sides. For a REGULAR shape, the symmetry count matches the full side count: 8.
16 doubles the side count. For a regular shape, symmetry lines equal the side count exactly: 8.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count the octagon's sides — that's also its symmetry-line count.

takeaways: A regular shape has as many symmetry lines as it has sides.
Non-regular shapes can have fewer — a rectangle has only 2, an isosceles triangle only 1.
A shape with no matching sides anywhere has zero lines of symmetry.
steps.teaser: next: spotting symmetry in letters and everyday objects.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **A regular shape's symmetry count matches its side count.** A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides, so it has 5 lines of symmetry — one through each corner and the midpoint of the opposite side.

explanationVariants: 5 equal sides give 5 lines of symmetry.
The side count and symmetry count match for regular shapes.

widget.prompt: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

options.feedback: 2 is too few for a regular shape with 5 equal sides. It has 5 symmetry lines.
10 doubles the side count. For a regular shape, symmetry lines equal the sides: 5.
